entities.summary:
Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a towering figure of the French Renaissance, was a polymathic scholar whose profound humanistic endeavors reshaped intellectual life in early 16th-century France. As a royal librarian, diplomat, and advisor to King Francis I, Budé championed the rigorous study of Greek and Latin antiquity, directly challenging the scholastic traditions prevalent in medieval universities. His advocacy for a new philological approach to ancient texts and legal codes laid foundational groundwork for modern scholarship and significantly influenced the nascent French educational system.

Budé's intellectual contributions spanned multiple disciplines. His seminal work, *De Asse et Partibus Eius* (1514), a meticulous study of ancient Roman coinage and weights, established him as a leading numismatist and economic historian, revealing the practical applications of classical learning. He also produced *Annotationes in XXIV libros Pandectarum* (1508), a critical philological commentary on Justinian's Pandects, which revolutionized the study of Roman law by applying humanist principles to legal texts, moving beyond the glossators' interpretations. Crucially, Budé was instrumental in persuading King Francis I to establish the *Collegium Trilingue* (later the Collège de France) in 1530, a groundbreaking institution dedicated to teaching Greek, Latin, and Hebrew outside the Sorbonne's conservative control, thus fostering a new generation of humanists and scholars.
